summary.text: Let \(x_*\in(1/2,1)\) satisfy \(H(x_*)=x_*\log 2=:c\), where \(H\) is binary entropy; bounding each residue by both \(2^k\) and \(\binom nk\le e^{nH(k/n)}\) gives \(a(n)\le n e^{nc}\). For \(k=\lfloor x_*n\rfloor+1\), entropy bounds show \(\binom nk<2^k\), so this unreduced summand is at least \(e^{nH(k/n)}/(n+1)\); since \(k/n\to x_*\), these bounds squeeze \(\log a(n)/n\to c\), and hence the nth roots tend to \(e^c\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=1}^n r_{n,k},\qquad
r_{n,k}:=\binom nk\bmod 2^k,
\]
where the residue is the least nonnegative residue. We prove that \(a(n)^{1/n}\) converges. In fact, we identify its limit in terms of a number \(x_*\in(1/2,1)\).

Define the binary entropy function
\[
H(x)=-x\log x-(1-x)\log(1-x)\qquad (0<x<1),
\]
with its continuous endpoint values \(H(0)=H(1)=0\). We will use the following standard facts. The function \(H\) is continuous on \([0,1]\), satisfies
\[
H(1/2)=\log 2,\qquad H(1)=0,
\]
and is strictly decreasing on \([1/2,1]\). Indeed, in the interior,
\[
H'(x)=\log\frac{1-x}{x},
\]
which is negative for \(x>1/2\).

Consider the continuous function
\[
g(x)=H(x)-x\log 2.
\]
At the two relevant endpoints,
\[
g(1/2)=\frac12\log 2>0,
\qquad
g(1)=-\log 2<0.
\]
The intermediate value theorem therefore gives a number
\[
\frac12<x_*<1
\]
such that
\[
H(x_*)=x_*\log 2.
\]
Set
\[
c:=x_*\log 2=H(x_*).
\]
In particular, \(c>0\). (The strict decrease of \(H\), together with the strict increase of \(x\log2\), also shows that this \(x_*\) is unique, although uniqueness is not needed for existence of the limit.) For every \(y\in[x_*,1]\), monotonicity gives
\[
H(y)\le H(x_*)=c. \tag{1}
\]
Moreover, if \(x_*<y\le1\), then strict monotonicity and \(\log2>0\) give
\[
H(y)<H(x_*)=x_*\log2<y\log2. \tag{2}
\]

We next establish the binomial coefficient estimates needed below. For integers \(n\ge1\) and \(0<k<n\), define, for \(0\le j\le n\),
\[
T_j=\binom nj k^j(n-k)^{n-j}.
\]
The binomial theorem gives
\[
\sum_{j=0}^nT_j=(k+(n-k))^n=n^n. \tag{3}
\]
The terms have a mode at \(j=k\). To see this without dividing by possibly inconvenient factors, use
\[
T_{j+1}(j+1)(n-k)=T_j(n-j)k. \tag{4}
\]
If \(j+1\le k\), then
\[
(j+1)(n-k)\le(n-j)k,
\]
and since \((j+1)(n-k)>0\), (4) implies \(T_j\le T_{j+1}\). If \(k\le j<n\), the inequality between the two factors reverses, and (4) implies \(T_{j+1}\le T_j\). Thus every \(T_j\) is at most
\[
T_k=\binom nk k^k(n-k)^{n-k}.
\]
Since this is one of the nonnegative terms in (3), while (3) contains \(n+1\) terms, we have the two-sided estimate
\[
T_k\le n^n\le(n+1)T_k. \tag{5}
\]

For \(0<k<n\), direct expansion of the entropy shows
\[
\exp\!\left(nH\!\left(\frac kn\right)\right)
 =\frac{n^n}{k^k(n-k)^{n-k}}. \tag{6}
\]
Indeed,
\[
nH(k/n)=n\log n-k\log k-(n-k)\log(n-k),
\]
and exponentiation yields (6). Dividing (5) by the positive quantity \(k^k(n-k)^{n-k}\), and using (6), gives
\[
\frac1{n+1}\exp\!\left(nH\!\left(\frac kn\right)\right)
\le \binom nk
\le \exp\!\left(nH\!\left(\frac kn\right)\right). \tag{7}
\]
This elementary entropy estimate is the source of both the upper and lower bounds for \(a(n)\).

We first bound every summand from above. Fix \(n\ge1\) and \(1\le k\le n\). There are two main cases.

If \(k\le x_*n\), then a least nonnegative residue modulo \(2^k\) is strictly less than \(2^k\). Hence
\[
r_{n,k}<2^k
 =\exp(k\log2)
 \le\exp(nx_*\log2)
 =\exp(nc). \tag{8}
\]

Suppose instead that \(k>x_*n\). If \(k=n\), then \(\binom nn=1<2^n\), so \(r_{n,n}=1\le e^{nc}\), since \(c>0\). If \(k<n\), then \(k/n\in[x_*,1]\), and (1) and the upper half of (7) give
\[
r_{n,k}\le\binom nk
\le\exp\!\left(nH\!\left(\frac kn\right)\right)
\le\exp(nc). \tag{9}
\]
Thus in all cases
\[
r_{n,k}\le e^{nc}.
\]
There are exactly \(n\) indices in the defining sum, so
\[
a(n)\le n e^{nc}. \tag{10}
\]
Also, for every \(n\ge1\), the term with \(k=n\) equals \(1\), so
\[
a(n)\ge1. \tag{11}
\]
In particular, taking logarithms will cause no difficulty.

For the matching lower bound, choose an integer just to the right of the critical proportion:
\[
k_n:=\lfloor x_*n\rfloor+1.
\]
It satisfies
\[
x_*n<k_n\le x_*n+1, \tag{12}
\]
and therefore
\[
x_*<\frac{k_n}{n}\le x_*+\frac1n \qquad(n\ge1). \tag{13}
\]
Because \(x_*<1\), we also have \(k_n<n\) for all sufficiently large \(n\): for example, (12) shows this as soon as \(n(1-x_*)>1\). Clearly \(k_n\ge1\).

For such sufficiently large \(n\), put \(y_n=k_n/n\). Then \(x_*<y_n<1\), so (2) gives
\[
H(y_n)<y_n\log2.
\]
Multiplying by \(n>0\) and exponentiating,
\[
\exp(nH(y_n))<\exp(k_n\log2)=2^{k_n}. \tag{14}
\]
By the upper estimate in (7),
\[
\binom n{k_n}\le e^{nH(y_n)}<2^{k_n}. \tag{15}
\]
Consequently reduction modulo \(2^{k_n}\) does nothing to this particular binomial coefficient:
\[
r_{n,k_n}=\binom n{k_n}. \tag{16}
\]
Since all summands in \(a(n)\) are nonnegative, (16), followed by the lower estimate in (7), yields
\[
a(n)\ge \binom n{k_n}
\ge\frac{e^{nH(k_n/n)}}{n+1}. \tag{17}
\]
This is the crucial lower bound: the index is chosen just beyond the point where the entropy bound drops below the modulus bound, ensuring that the selected binomial coefficient survives unchanged as a residue.

We now pass to exponential growth rates. From (13), the squeeze theorem gives
\[
\frac{k_n}{n}\longrightarrow x_*.
\]
Continuity of \(H\) therefore implies
\[
H\!\left(\frac{k_n}{n}\right)\longrightarrow H(x_*)=c. \tag{18}
\]
Taking logarithms in (17) and (10), and dividing by \(n\), gives, for all sufficiently large \(n\),
\[
H\!\left(\frac{k_n}{n}\right)-\frac{\log(n+1)}n
\le \frac{\log a(n)}n
\le c+\frac{\log n}{n}. \tag{19}
\]
The familiar sublinear growth of the logarithm gives
\[
\frac{\log n}{n}\longrightarrow0,
\qquad
\frac{\log(n+1)}n\longrightarrow0. \tag{20}
\]
Combining (18)–(20) with (19), the squeeze theorem proves
\[
\frac{\log a(n)}n\longrightarrow c. \tag{21}
\]

Finally, because \(a(n)>0\), the positive real \(n\)-th root can be written as
\[
a(n)^{1/n}
=\exp\!\left(\frac{\log a(n)}n\right).
\]
The exponential function is continuous, so (21) gives
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}a(n)^{1/n}=e^c.
\]
Since \(c=x_*\log2\), the limit may equivalently be written
\[
e^c=2^{x_*},
\]
where \(x_*\in(1/2,1)\) is the solution of
\[
H(x_*)=x_*\log2.
\]
In particular, the asserted limit exists.
